data.cultural_impact: The name "Restituta" holds historical and cultural significance as the name of several saints in Christian tradition. Among them is St. Restituta of Córdoba, who was a virgin martyr during the time of persecution under Emperor Diocletian. She was discovered hiding in a tomb and subsequently brought before the emperor for judgment. Despite being mocked and tortured, she remained steadfast in her faith. Finally, she was condemned to death by being burned in an iron furnace. But God protected her, miraculously preserving her from harm. Thus, she is the patron saint of relics, tombs, and miraculous recoveries. Another saint associated with this name is St. Restituta of Ipswich, who is said to have been returned to miraculous life almost three centuries after her death. These stories illustrate courage and faith in the face of adversity, providing a cultural legacy and inspiring generations.
data.spiritual_significance: The name "Restituta" carries profound spiritual significance through its origins, symbolizing restoration, renewal, and redemption. In the Christian context, it serves as a reminder of God's power to restore, redeem, and renew both spiritually and physically. Restituta is a testament to the power of faith in times of trial and the assurance of a divine reward. Its spiritual essence invites us to embrace the idea that no matter how bleak or challenging our circumstances may be, God is capable of transforming our lives in miraculous ways. The name is rooted in the biblical theme of restoration, which can be found throughout the Old Testament and culminates in the New Testament with the message of salvation and the promise of eternal life.

historical_references.reference: The earliest known record of a Christian named Restituta is from the Catacombs of Priscilla in Rome, dating from the late 2nd to early 3rd century AD. Restituta is believed to have been a young virgin who was martyred during the persecution of Christians during the Roman Empire. Her name means 'restored' or 'redeemed'.

The second historical reference comes from the martyrology of St. Hippolytus of Rome, written in the late 3rd or early 4th century AD. Restituta is mentioned along with her mother Quintilla and her sister Marcellina, who were also martyred for their faith in Rome during the reign of the Emperor Trajan Decius. The three women were buried in the Catacomb of San Callisto.
